stem: A client is starting inhaled fluticasone for maintenance asthma therapy. Which instruction helps reduce a common local adverse effect?

options.A: Use fluticasone when acute wheezing begins, then rinse the mouth afterward because inhaled corticosteroids also provide rapid rescue bronchodilation.
options.B: Swallow water after each inhaled dose so medication left in the mouth reaches the stomach and continues the intended anti-inflammatory effect.
options.C: Rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after each inhaled dose to help reduce the risk of oropharyngeal candidiasis.
options.D: Avoid a prescribed valved holding chamber because using one increases oral deposition and raises the likelihood of corticosteroid-related thrush.

rationale: Current DailyMed labeling directs patients to rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after inhaled fluticasone to reduce the risk of oropharyngeal candidiasis. The medication is maintenance therapy and is not indicated for acute bronchospasm. A therefore misuses fluticasone as rescue therapy, B incorrectly instructs the client to swallow the rinse, and D contradicts labeling that allows a valved holding chamber in appropriate patients.
educational_objective: Teach clients using inhaled fluticasone to rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after each dose to reduce oropharyngeal candidiasis risk.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine
source_document_title: Fluticasone Propionate Inhalation Aerosol — Prescribing Information
source_locator: Dosage and Administration 2.1 Administration Information: after inhalation rinse mouth with water without swallowing to reduce oropharyngeal candidiasis risk. Warnings and Precautions 5.1 Oropharyngeal Candidiasis repeats the instruction. Indications and Usage: not indicated for relief of acute bronchospasm. A valved holding chamber and mask may be used in appropriate young patients.
source_claim_supported: Rinsing the mouth with water without swallowing after inhaled fluticasone reduces oropharyngeal candidiasis risk; fluticasone is not rescue therapy for acute bronchospasm.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed pp. 38–41: provide medication education, identify adverse effects, and safely administer inhaled medications.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — inhaled corticosteroid teaching
correction_summary: Removed the absolute-word cue and rebuilt the distractors as parallel errors involving rescue misuse, swallowing the rinse, and incorrect spacer teaching.

audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — fluticasone is not indicated for rapid rescue of acute bronchospasm.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — labeling specifies rinse without swallowing.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS — directly matches current labeling and is uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — labeling permits a valved holding chamber in appropriate patients.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — no absolute-word distractor pattern remains.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether mouth rinsing is merely optional hygiene; current prescribing information explicitly recommends it to reduce candidiasis risk.
